tasks.short: Explain how to complete and submit lab reports, answer students' questions, update the submission guide, post it with the deadlines and remind students.

steps.what: Teaching assistant informs students of the procedures for completing lab reports in the lab session
Teaching assistant answers students' e-mails about formats and deadlines
Teaching assistant updates the guide for submitting lab reports
Teaching assistant checks the final guide before publishing: steps and formats match the lecturer's requirements, deadlines are the lecturer's, and it goes to this class
Teaching assistant publishes the guide and deadlines to the class: by e-mail today, by one release on the course page after the change
Teaching assistant checks the deadline notices before scheduling: each date matches the lecturer's deadline, the text is right, and they go to this class
Teaching assistant reminds students of upcoming deadlines: by e-mail today; after the change by one scheduled release of the platform's deadline notices

tasks.design: The course page in the learning platform ({LMS}) holds the submission guide, a short FAQ and the assignment dates, so students find most answers before they e-mail. The teaching assistant checks the updated guide and publishes it once to the class, then checks the deadline notices built from the assignment dates and schedules them once. Explaining in the lab and answering the remaining questions stay with the teaching assistant.
tasks.previous_blocker: The guide was sent by e-mail each term and the same questions came in again and again.
tasks.enabler_now: Learning platforms hold guides, FAQs and assignment dates with automatic notices.
tasks.still_hard: Students skip the guide; some questions still come by e-mail.
tasks.human_edge: Showing a confused student what a good results section looks like.

reach.learn: Whether one guide per course cuts late or wrong submissions.

evidence.claim: Learning platforms hold guides, FAQs and assignment dates and send notices from those dates.
Schools need a processor agreement and a DPIA before student data go into online tools.

assumptions: Boundary: from course requirements to deadline notices; grading is outside.
Input contract: requirements and deadlines set by the lecturer; fallback is e-mail.
Explaining in the lab keeps its full time. s3 keeps 90: dates fill from the assignment dates, but rewriting the guide stays. Checking and releasing the guide and the notices are their own steps.

already_counted.description: Teaching assistant checks the updated guide.

incremental.description: Teaching assistant adds new questions to the FAQ.

approvals.approved_version: The submission guide and deadlines exactly as checked by the teaching assistant in s3b, published once to this class's course page; changes need a new check before publishing.

The deadline notices with the dates and text exactly as checked by the teaching assistant in s4b, sent by the platform to this class on the scheduled days; a changed deadline needs a new check before notices go out.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: most e-mails are about content the FAQ cannot answer (s2 85) (16.2); high: a large first-year course with many format and deadline e-mails (23.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Collect graded work from the graders, check all work is graded before the deadline, get the lecturer's sign-off, return digital assignments with feedback, and hand back paper assignments in the lab.

steps.what: Teaching assistant collects graded work from the graders by e-mail
Teaching assistant checks all work is graded before the established deadlines
Lecturer signs off the graded work for release
Teaching assistant checks the release batch: every submission graded, grades match the lecturer's signed-off list, feedback attached to the right student
Teaching assistant returns graded digital assignments and feedback to students: one e-mail per student today, by one release in the assessment tool after the change
Teaching assistant hands back paper assignments in the lab before the deadline

tasks.design: Graders mark digital submissions in the assessment tool ({LMS}), so graded work is not collected by e-mail. A progress view shows which submissions are still ungraded as the deadline nears. Once the lecturer has signed off, the teaching assistant checks the batch and releases graded work and feedback once from the tool instead of one e-mail per student. Paper lab reports, about 30% of assignments, are still collected from graders and handed back in the lab. Recording marks and answering grade questions are separate tasks and not counted here.
tasks.previous_blocker: Graded work came by e-mail from several graders and was returned one e-mail at a time.
tasks.enabler_now: Assessment tools let several graders mark in one place and release results.
tasks.still_hard: Graders who mark offline still need their marks entered.
tasks.human_edge: Handing back a weak report with advice on what to do next time.

reach.learn: Whether one tool shortens marking rounds.

evidence.claim: Digital assessment platforms can grade closed questions, split open ones across markers and run item analysis.
The exam board appoints the examiners who set results.

assumptions: Boundary: from graded work to assignments returned; recording marks and answering grade questions are separate tasks.
Input contract: graders mark in the assessment tool; release signed off by the lecturer; fallback is e-mail.
Scenario: about 70% of assignments are submitted and graded in the tool; the rest are paper lab reports.
Lecturer time is outside the teaching assistant's savings.
research_questions: Are assignments returned before the deadline more often?

already_counted.description: Teaching assistant reads the progress view.

incremental.description: Teaching assistant sets up assignments and grader access in the tool.

approvals.approved_version: The grades signed off by the lecturer in s3 and each student's feedback, exactly as checked by the teaching assistant in s3b, returned once through the assessment tool to each student; a changed grade needs a new sign-off and check before release.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: half of assignments stay on paper (s1 60, s4 55) (26.9); high: about 70% are graded in the tool as assumed (43.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Write exam questions, get the lecturer's approval, build the exam, arrange provisions such as extra time, proctor the exam and collect the papers.

steps.what: Teaching assistant writes exam questions from the course objectives

loop.input: The course objectives, the lecture slides and earlier exams; no student data.
loop.output: Draft exam questions, each tagged to an objective, with an answer key.
loop.check: Code rejects questions without an objective tag or key and flags any that repeat earlier exams word for word; the teaching assistant then checks each question's facts against the lecture material, works out each answer to confirm the key, and confirms the question tests its tagged objective, editing or dropping any that fail.
loop.stop: Approved by the teaching assistant, or after two redrafts the teaching assistant writes the questions.
loop.why_not_simpler: New questions per objective need free text; a fixed bank runs out.

steps.what: Lecturer approves the exam questions
Teaching assistant builds the exam: formatting and printing today; setting sections and timing in the assessment tool after the change
Teaching assistant arranges extra time and other exam provisions
Teaching assistant proctors the examinations in the exam hall
Teaching assistant collects and counts papers and notes absent students

tasks.design: A bounded step drafts exam questions per course objective with an answer key, and the teaching assistant edits every question before the lecturer approves the exam. The approved exam is built in the digital assessment tool ({LMS}), which applies extra time from the student records ({OTHER}) and records who submitted. Proctoring stays with people; no AI proctoring.
tasks.previous_blocker: Questions were written from scratch, exams printed and provisions arranged by e-mail.
tasks.enabler_now: Language models draft questions from objectives, and digital exam tools apply provisions.
tasks.still_hard: Drafted questions can test the wrong thing; editing takes care.
tasks.human_edge: Noticing a student in distress during the exam.
tasks.altitude: The teaching assistant edits drafted questions instead of writing them all.

reach.learn: Whether provisions from records cut errors.

evidence.claim: In a randomised trial, teachers using Aila spent 49 minutes less a week on lesson preparation with quality no worse.
AI used for test proctoring or evaluating learning outcomes is high-risk; this design uses neither.

assumptions: Boundary: from course objectives to the attendance record; grading is outside.
Input contract: objectives set by the lecturer; provisions from the student records kept by student administration; fallback is writing and printing by hand.
Lecturer time is outside the teaching assistant's savings.
s3 keeps 20 for setting up the exam in the tool. s6 keeps 10 for collecting the paper versions.
research_questions: How many drafted questions survive the lecturer's review?

already_counted.description: Teaching assistant edits every drafted question.
Teaching assistant checks the provisions applied.

incremental.description: Teaching assistant builds paper versions for students who need them.

approvals.approved_version: The exam questions and answer key as approved by the lecturer in s2; any changed question needs a new approval before the exam is built.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a small course with a paper exam and provisions arranged by hand (s3 80, s4 80, s6 80) (15.8); high: a large course in the digital tool (33.2).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Spot students who need extra help from quiz results, invite them to office hours, tutor them, prepare extra practice and keep short notes.

steps.what: Teaching assistant goes through quiz results to find students who need help
Teaching assistant checks the invitations before they go: each student is below the threshold on the named topic, the text is neutral and gives the office hours
Teaching assistant invites those students to office hours: one e-mail each today, by one release from the platform after the change
Teaching assistant tutors or mentors students who need additional instruction
Teaching assistant puts together extra practice on weak topics
Teaching assistant keeps notes on who came and what was covered

tasks.design: A results view in the learning platform ({LMS}) lists students below a score the lecturer sets, per topic; the teaching assistant reviews the list, checks the invitations and releases them once from the platform. Extra practice is assembled from the course question bank by weak topic, and the teaching assistant writes attendance and topics in a short note form instead of on paper. Tutoring stays in person; no AI judges students.
tasks.previous_blocker: Results were scanned by hand in spreadsheets and practice put together from scratch.
tasks.enabler_now: Learning platforms show results per topic and assemble practice from a bank.
tasks.still_hard: Students who need help most often do not come to office hours.
tasks.human_edge: Hearing that a student's grades dropped because of trouble at home.
tasks.altitude: The teaching assistant confirms a list instead of building it.

evidence.claim: Learning platforms show quiz results per topic and assemble practice from a question bank.
AI that evaluates learning outcomes to steer learning is high-risk from 2 December 2027; this design uses a fixed score threshold.

assumptions: Boundary: from quiz results to mentoring notes; formal study advice is outside.
Input contract: quiz results from the learning platform; score threshold set by the lecturer; question bank kept by the lecturer; fallback is spreadsheets.
Tutoring and notes keep their full time; notes are a first record. s1 keeps 40 because the results view lists students below the score.
Students' time is outside the teaching assistant's savings.
unknowns: Students below the threshold per quiz.
research_questions: Do invited students come to office hours?

already_counted.description: Teaching assistant confirms the help list.
Teaching assistant checks the assembled practice.

incremental.description: Teaching assistant tags bank questions by topic.

approvals.approved_version: The office-hour invitation text and the students on the help list exactly as checked by the teaching assistant in s1b, sent once from the platform to those students; added students or a changed text need a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a small group the teaching assistant knows well, so the view and bank add little (s1 80, s4 80) (10.1); high: a large course with weekly quizzes (22.1).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The teaching assistant keeps teaching, proctoring and mentoring; copying marks, e-mail rounds and writing questions from scratch shrink.
role.ambitious_version: A teaching assistant who spends saved hours in office hours.
